facts.text: Arctic sea ice usually reaches its largest extent in March and its smallest in September.
Satellites have measured Arctic sea ice continuously since the late 1970s; the record used here starts in 1979.
Sea ice extent counts every area of ocean where at least 15 percent of the surface is covered by ice.
From 1979 to 2024, September sea ice shrank by about 12.1 percent per decade, compared with the 1981–2010 average.
The March maximum shrank more slowly, by about 2.6 percent per decade, so summer ice is being lost about five times faster than winter ice.
On September 16, 2012, Arctic sea ice fell to 3.41 million square kilometers, the lowest extent in the satellite record.
The 2012 low was 760,000 square kilometers below the previous record, set on September 18, 2007, and 18 percent below it.
A strong storm formed off Alaska on August 5, 2012, moved into the central Arctic Ocean and broke a huge piece off the main ice cover.
The ice that broke away melted faster, which may have helped cause the 2012 record low.
Scientists said the storm itself was not extraordinary; the long-term weakening of the ice made a storm of that size far more damaging than it would have been decades earlier.
In the mid-1980s up to one third of the winter ice cover was thick ice that had survived several summers; by 2020 such ice made up only about 5 percent.
Sea ice reflects up to 80 percent of the sunlight that reaches it, while open ocean absorbs much more, warming the water and air and melting more ice.
The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the globe, and the loss of sea ice is one of the reasons.
Losing sea ice reduces the habitat of polar bears, walruses and seals.
Records of the distant past suggest that the recent decline of Arctic sea ice is unmatched in at least the last 1,500 years.
Between 1979–1988 and 2010–2019, Arctic sea ice area fell by about 40 percent in September and about 10 percent in March, mainly because of human influence.
The Arctic is likely to be practically free of sea ice in September at least once before 2050, meaning less than 1 million square kilometers of ice.
Derived from the OWID series: September 2012 (3.57 million km² as a monthly average) is the lowest September in 1979–2024; 2020 (4.00) is second and 2007 (4.27) third.

Derived from the OWID series: from 1979 to 2024 the September average fell from 7.05 to 4.35 million km² (a loss of about 38 percent), while the March average fell from 16.34 to 14.87 (about 9 percent).
